question.text: When photons of energy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>4</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>0</mn><mo> </mo><mi>eV</mi></math> fall on the surface of a metal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi></math>, the ejected photoelectrons have maximum kinetic energy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></msub></math> (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>eV</mi></math>) and a de-Broglie wavelength <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></msub></math>. When the same photons fall on the surface of another metal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>B</mi></math>, the maximum kinetic energy of ejected photoelectrons is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.5</mo><mo> </mo><mi>eV</mi></math>. If the de-Broglie wavelength of these photoelectrons is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></msub></math>, then the work function of metal <math> <mi>B</mi> </math> is

solution.text:
The relation between de-Broglie wavelength and kinetic energy is

λ=h2Kme
λAλB=KBKA⇒12=TA-1.5TA  ⇒TA=2 eV

⇒KB=2-1.5=0.5 eV

So, the work-function of B is
ϕB=4.0-0.5=3.5 eV
